claim_text: progressive summarization tend to lose? Exact numbers, percentages, dates, order IDs and customer-stated expectations
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.1-K1. Anthropic: 'overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context'; Claude Code docs: compaction keeps requests and key snippets but 'detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost'.

claim_text: A persistent 'case facts' block (amounts, dates, IDs, statuses) included in every prompt, outside the summarized history.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.1-S1. Docs: 'Use structured formats for state data' (JSON) and persist state outside the context window.

claim_text: Models use the start and end of long inputs most reliably. Put a key-findings summary first and use explicit section headers.
exam_vs_today_note: Liu et al. 2023 (TACL 2024) 'Lost in the Middle': multi-doc QA and key-value retrieval accuracy is U-shaped, highest when the relevant item is at the start or end, and drops in the middle even for long-context models (2023-era models). Anthropic docs confirm length-related 'context rot' and position sensitivity (long data at top, query at end: 'up to 30 percent' better). Mitigation = blueprint 5.1-S4.
fix: Optional: add a one-line source note ('Liu et al., 2023') so the learner knows it is an empirical finding, measured on 2023 models.

claim_text: Trim tool output to the relevant fields before it enters context, in the tool or in a PostToolUse hook.
exam_vs_today_note: Docs: PostToolUse 'updatedToolOutput' 'Replaces the tool's output with the provided value before it is sent to Claude' and works for all tools (updatedMCPToolOutput is MCP-only). Blueprint 5.1-S3 and 1.5. API alternative today: context editing clear_tool_uses_20250919 (not mentioned).

claim_text: Scratchpad files for key findings, Explore or other subagents for verbose discovery, phase summaries injected into new contexts, and /compact.
exam_vs_today_note: All four match blueprint 5.4 and still work. But current Claude Code auto-compacts, most models have 1M windows, and the best-practices page calls 'use subagents to protect your context window' old advice ('Running out of context is rarely the problem anymore'). m07 has no 'Real world today' callout, so a learner who reads current docs may doubt the exam answer.
fix: Add a 'Real world today' callout to m07 step 2: 'Claude Code now compacts automatically as the window nears its limit (/compact [focus] still works; /autocompact sets the threshold; /context shows usage). Most current models have a 1M-token window, and Claude delegates to subagents, including the built-in read-only Explore, on its own. Claude Code's best-practices page lists "manage the context window aggressively" and "use subagents to protect your context window" as older advice, while still recommending subagents to keep noisy output out of the main conversation. On the exam, still choose scratchpads, Explore/subagent delegation, phase summaries and /compact for 5.4.'

claim_text: Each agent exports state to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects the relevant state into agent prompts.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.4-K4/S4. Anthropic's long-running-harness article uses the same idea (claude-progress.txt + JSON feature list + git) so a fresh session recovers where the last stopped.

claim_text: A context window isn't a hard drive. Everything in it competes for the model's attention, and position matters.
exam_vs_today_note: Docs: 'more context isn't automatically better. As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot.' Context-engineering article: context is 'a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns'.

claim_text: 'Customer was promised a $247.83 refund on order #8812 by Friday' becomes 'customer discussed a refund.'
exam_vs_today_note: Illustrative example inside quotes; consistent with documented compaction loss.

claim_text: An order lookup returns 40+ fields; the return workflow needs 5. Over twenty turns, that's most of your context.
exam_vs_today_note: 40+/5 is the blueprint's example (5.1-K3). 'Most of your context' is unlabeled and depends on payload size; with 200K–1M windows twenty lookups rarely fill most of the window, though they can be most of the tokens sent (the widget shows ~83% at 24 turns, labeled illustrative).
fix: 'An order lookup returns 40+ fields; the return workflow needs 5. Over twenty turns, those unused fields can become most of the tokens you send on every turn (illustrative).'

claim_text: Models reliably use the beginning and end of long inputs and may miss findings buried in the middle.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.1-K2 wording; supported by Liu et al. 2023. 'May miss' is appropriately hedged. Current Anthropic docs describe general context rot rather than a U-shape specifically.

claim_text: Three valid escalation triggers? The customer explicitly asks for a human; policy is ambiguous or silent on the request (or an exception is needed); the agent can't make meaningful progress.
exam_vs_today_note: Matches blueprint 5.2-K1. Anthropic docs define only an escalation-accuracy metric (≥95%), no trigger list; nothing contradicts.

claim_text: Customer demands a human for a simple issue. Escalate immediately. Don't investigate first or try to talk them out of it.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-S2.

claim_text: Frustrated customer, simple issue, no request for a human? Acknowledge the frustration and offer the resolution. Escalate if they reiterate
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K2/S3.

claim_text: Why not escalate on sentiment or self-rated confidence? ... LLM self-confidence is poorly calibrated: wrong answers are often confident.
exam_vs_today_note: Front is scoped to escalation (5.2-K3, fine). Back generalizes to all LLM self-confidence. Research is mixed: Xiong et al. 2023 find verbalized confidence tends to be overconfident; Kadavath et al. 2022 find larger models 'well-calibrated' on MC/true-false in the right format; Tian et al. 2023 find RLHF models' verbalized confidence often better calibrated than token probabilities. The unqualified rule conflicts with 5.5-S3 calibrated field-level confidence.
fix: 'Sentiment doesn't measure complexity, and a raw self-rating isn't calibrated: an agent can be confidently wrong on exactly the hard cases. (Field-level confidence calibrated on labeled data is fine for routing review; see 5.5.)'

claim_text: Lookup returns three matching customers? Ask for an additional identifier. Never pick by heuristic.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K4/S5; 'never' matches blueprint ('rather than heuristic selection').

claim_text: 97% overall accuracy. Safe to cut human review? Not yet. Check accuracy by document type and field first, then keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence output.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.5-K1/K2/K4. Stratification by segment is standard sampling practice (separate per-stratum estimates).

claim_text: Two credible sources give different statistics? Keep both with attribution and annotate the conflict. Include dates
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.6-K3/K4.

claim_text: Route work to them when it changes the outcome, not when the agent feels uneasy.
exam_vs_today_note: Module principle covers 5.5 too, where blueprint 5.5-S4 routes 'low model confidence' extractions to human review. 'Not when the agent feels uneasy' reads as rejecting confidence-based routing in general. Anthropic's own research prompt asks Claude to 'Track your confidence levels... to improve calibration'.
fix: 'Route work to them when it changes the outcome, using explicit criteria or calibrated signals, not the agent's raw gut feel.'

claim_text: The customer explicitly asks for a human. Honor it immediately, without investigating first or trying to talk them out of it.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-S2.

claim_text: Policy is ambiguous or silent on this specific request, or an exception is needed. A gap in policy isn't permission to improvise.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K1/S4.

claim_text: The agent can't make meaningful progress.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K1.

claim_text: A customer who demands a person gets one. A customer who is frustrated about a simple problem... gets acknowledgement and an offer to fix it now, and is escalated if they say again that they want a person.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K2/S3.

claim_text: Sentiment. Anger isn't complexity. A furious customer with a tracking question is a simple case.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K3. Note: Anthropic's support guide tracks sentiment as a quality metric, not as an escalation trigger; no conflict.

claim_text: Self-reported confidence ('rate yourself 1–10'). The agent that's mishandling hard cases is usually confident about them.
exam_vs_today_note: F8. Blueprint 5.2-K3 says only 'unreliable proxy'. The official sample rationale says the agent in that scenario is incorrectly confident on hard cases, but 'usually' generalizes it. Research: verbalized confidence skews high (Xiong et al. 2023) but carries real signal and can be calibrated (Kadavath et al. 2022; Tian et al. 2023). The overstatement sets up rejection of 5.5 confidence routing.
fix: 'Self-reported confidence ("rate yourself 1–10"). A raw self-rating doesn't measure case complexity, and an agent can be confidently wrong on exactly the hard cases it mishandles. (Calibrated field-level confidence for review routing is different; see below.)'

claim_text: explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt with few-shot examples of escalate versus resolve. Try that before building classifiers.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-S1. Docs: few-shot examples are 'one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output'.

claim_text: When a lookup returns several matching customers, ask for another identifier (email, order number, postal code). Never choose by heuristic.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2-K4/S5.

claim_text: explicit request -> Escalate now; late package + credit in policy -> Resolve; 3 accounts -> Ask; damaged item with photo -> Resolve ('Escalating it lowers first-contact resolution')
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.2. Support guide tracks deflection/resolution metrics.

claim_text: gift-wrap fee refund; 'policy covers product refunds only' -> 'Escalate: policy gap' ('Policy is silent on this request')
exam_vs_today_note: 'Covers product refunds only' reads as an explicit exclusion, not silence; a careful learner could sort it as 'deny/resolve'. Blueprint 5.2-S4 is about ambiguous or silent policy.
fix: 'Customer wants the gift-wrap fee refunded because the wrapping was torn; the policy covers product refunds and says nothing about fees.'

claim_text: Aggregate accuracy hides weak segments. 97% overall can include 80% on handwritten forms or one critical field.

claim_text: Have the model output a confidence for each field, then set review thresholds using a labeled validation set. Raw scores mean nothing until calibrated.
exam_vs_today_note: First two sentences = blueprint 5.5-S3 (correct). 'Mean nothing' overstates: raw scores carry ranking signal (Kadavath et al. 2022; Tian et al. 2023); what they lack is a reliable mapping to accuracy.
fix: 'Raw scores aren't probabilities until calibrated: a 0.9 may not mean 90% correct.'

claim_text: Stratified random sampling. Even after automating, keep sampling high-confidence extractions across segments to measure error rates and catch new error patterns.
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.5-K2/S1. Per-stratum sampling gives segment-level error estimates.

claim_text: Send low-confidence fields and ambiguous or contradictory source documents to reviewers first
exam_vs_today_note: Blueprint 5.5-S4.

claim_text: Raw self-rated confidence as an escalation trigger is a trap. Field-level confidence calibrated against labeled data and used to prioritize review is good practice. The difference is calibration.
exam_vs_today_note: Mostly right (it resolves F8 in-lesson). Last sentence is imprecise: blueprint 5.2-K3 rejects self-reported confidence as a proxy for case complexity regardless of calibration; the differences are purpose (complexity proxy vs prioritizing field review) and calibration.
fix: '...The differences are what it's used for (prioritizing review of extracted fields, not judging case complexity) and whether it's calibrated on labeled data.'

claim_text: '97.0% accurate overall'; by type 99.1% (6,200), 98.4% (2,900), 81.7% (900); by field 99.3, 98.6, 98.9, 74.2; '10,000 extracted documents last quarter'
exam_vs_today_note: F11 confirmed. Weighted mean of the type breakdown = (6200×99.1+2900×98.4+900×81.7)/10000 = 97.33%, not 97.0%. The field rates average 92.75% (and a document-level 'all fields correct' rate would be ≤74.2%), so they can't produce 97% under either reading. No 'illustrative' label anywhere in the widget (contextBudget has one).
fix: Change headline to '97.3% accurate overall (document-weighted)'. Add caption: 'Numbers are illustrative. Field rates are measured on the documents where each field appears (tax ID appears mostly on handwritten forms).' Or change Tax ID to appear on 900 docs and say so.
